Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

\[
\boxed{499}
\]

Let  
\[
D=\{1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250\}
\]
be the set of positive divisors of \(250\).

We first extract the forced structure of the sets \(A_d\) for \(d\in D\).

---

## 1. Structure forced by the divisor sets

For every positive integer \(i\),

\[
|A_i|=|A_i\cap A_i|=\gcd(i,i)=i.
\]

Also, if \(g=\gcd(i,j)\), then \(A_g\subseteq A_i\cap A_j\). Since

\[
|A_g|=g=|A_i\cap A_j|,
\]

we have the stronger identity

\[
A_i\cap A_j=A_{\gcd(i,j)}. \tag{1}
\]

In particular, if \(d\mid e\), then

\[
A_d=A_d\cap A_e\subseteq A_e.
\]

Now consider an element \(x\in A_{250}\). Let

\[
E_x=\{d\in D:x\in A_d\}.
\]

Because of (1), if \(x\in A_i\) and \(x\in A_j\), then \(x\in A_{\gcd(i,j)}\). Thus the smallest divisor in \(E_x\) is well-defined; call it \(m(x)\). One checks that

\[
x\in A_d \iff m(x)\mid d.
\]

Therefore the elements of \(A_{250}\) split into blocks

\[
B_m=\{x\in A_{250}:m(x)=m\},\qquad m\in D,
\]

and for every \(d\in D\),

\[
A_d=\bigsqcup_{m\mid d}B_m.
\]

Since \(|A_d|=d\), we get

\[
\sum_{m\mid d}|B_m|=d.
\]

Solving recursively gives

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
m&1&2&5&10&25&50&125&250\\ \hline
|B_m|&1&1&4&4&20&20&100&100
\end{array}
\]

These are exactly the values \(\varphi(m)\).

---

## 2. Normalizing the labels

We may assume that

\[
A_{250}=\{1,2,\dots,250\}.
\]

Indeed, if \(A_{250}=\{s_1<s_2<\cdots<s_{250}\}\), apply a permutation of the positive integers sending \(s_r\mapsto r\) and sending the complement of \(A_{250}\) to the complement of \(\{1,\dots,250\}\). This preserves all intersection sizes. For \(d\mid 250\), since \(A_d\subseteq A_{250}\), its maximum can only decrease or stay the same.

Now define, for \(t=1,2,\dots,250\),

\[
N_t=\#\{d\in D:\max A_d\ge t\}.
\]

Then

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d=\sum_{t=1}^{250}N_t. \tag{2}
\]

Fix \(t\). Let

\[
H_t=A_{250}\cap\{t,t+1,\dots,250\},
\]

so

\[
|H_t|=251-t.
\]

Let

\[
T_t=\{m\in D:B_m\cap H_t\neq\varnothing\}.
\]

Then

\[
N_t=\#\{d\in D:\exists m\in T_t\text{ with }m\mid d\}.
\]

Let

\[
C_t=\bigcup_{m\in T_t}\{d\in D:m\mid d\}.
\]

The set \(C_t\) is an “up-set” in the divisor lattice: if \(d\in C_t\) and \(d\mid e\) with \(e\mid 250\), then \(e\in C_t\).

Also,

\[
|H_t|\le \sum_{m\in T_t}|B_m|=\sum_{m\in T_t}\varphi(m).
\]

Since \(T_t\subseteq C_t\),

\[
|H_t|\le \sum_{m\in C_t}\varphi(m).
\]

---

## 3. Maximizing \(\sum_{m\in C}\varphi(m)\) over up-sets

Arrange the divisors as

\[
\begin{matrix}
1&2\\
5&10\\
25&50\\
125&250
\end{matrix}
\]

where divisibility moves right or upward. An up-set is closed to the right and upward.

Let \(c_b\) be the number of chosen elements in the row containing \(5^b,2\cdot 5^b\), for \(b=0,1,2,3\). Then

\[
0\le c_0\le c_1\le c_2\le c_3\le 2,
\]

and

\[
\sum_{m\in C}\varphi(m)=c_0+4c_1+20c_2+100c_3.
\]

For a fixed size \(k\), this is maximized by filling from the top down. The maximum values are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
k&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\ \hline
\max\limits_{\substack{C\text{ up-set}\\ |C|=k}}\sum_{m\in C}\varphi(m)
&100&200&220&240&244&248&249&250
\end{array}
\]

Denote these maxima by \(W_1,\dots,W_8\), and set \(W_0=0\).

Now, if \(N_t\le r\), then

\[
|H_t|\le W_r.
\]

Equivalently, if

\[
W_{r-1}<|H_t|\le W_r,
\]

then \(N_t\ge r\).

Since \(|H_t|=251-t\), this gives:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
t & |H_t| & N_t\ge \\ \hline
151\le t\le 250 & 1\le |H_t|\le 100 & 1\\
51\le t\le 150 & 101\le |H_t|\le 200 & 2\\
31\le t\le 50 & 201\le |H_t|\le 220 & 3\\
11\le t\le 30 & 221\le |H_t|\le 240 & 4\\
7\le t\le 10 & 241\le |H_t|\le 244 & 5\\
3\le t\le 6 & 245\le |H_t|\le 248 & 6\\
t=2 & 249 & 7\\
t=1 & 250 & 8
\end{array}
\]

Therefore, using (2),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d
&\ge 100\cdot1+100\cdot2+20\cdot3+20\cdot4\\
&\qquad +4\cdot5+4\cdot6+1\cdot7+1\cdot8\\
&=100+200+60+80+20+24+7+8\\
&=499.
\end{aligned}
\]

So every valid sequence has sum at least \(499\).

---

## 4. Construction attaining \(499\)

We now construct a sequence achieving the bound.

Choose pairwise disjoint sets \(B_n\) of positive integers with

\[
|B_n|=\varphi(n).
\]

For the divisors of \(250\), choose specifically:

\[
\begin{aligned}
B_1&=\{1\},\\
B_2&=\{2\},\\
B_5&=\{3,4,5,6\},\\
B_{10}&=\{7,8,9,10\},\\
B_{25}&=\{11,12,\dots,30\},\\
B_{50}&=\{31,32,\dots,50\},\\
B_{125}&=\{51,52,\dots,150\},\\
B_{250}&=\{151,152,\dots,250\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For all other \(n\), choose any unused positive integers in blocks of size \(\varphi(n)\).

Define

\[
A_i=\bigsqcup_{n\mid i}B_n.
\]

Then

\[
A_i\cap A_j=\bigsqcup_{n\mid \gcd(i,j)}B_n,
\]

so

\[
|A_i\cap A_j|
=\sum_{n\mid \gcd(i,j)}\varphi(n)
=\gcd(i,j).
\]

Thus the sequence is valid.

Now compute the required maxima:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d&1&2&5&10&25&50&125&250\\ \hline
\max A_d&1&2&6&10&30&50&150&250
\end{array}
\]

Hence

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d
=1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250
=499.
\]

Therefore the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]
